title: Karma Yoga
hook: a quiet desert inside a rush-hour street, and the week's last look at the yoga of work
carry: a desert in the busy street

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karma Yoga and the parking lot: character lives in the common actions, each one leaving an impression. Which ordinary thing did you do as if it counted? Day nine hundred forty-five.

Where would you go to find silence? A cave, a retreat, an empty chapel on a weekday, a desert. In his talks on Karma Yoga, Vivekananda moves the desert. He sets it down in the streets of a big city, in all their traffic. Picture it today as a train station at rush hour, announcements overhead, someone running for a door that's already closing. Busy hands, and somewhere inside, a desert. He calls the person who can hold both an ideal. It's a fitting place to end the week, because it gathers what the yoga of work has been saying.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU GO FOR SILENCE?` → `HE MOVES THE DESERT.` → `INTO THE STATION AT RUSH HOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the ideal, in his own picture. The ideal person, Vivekananda says, is one who, in the deepest silence and solitude, finds intense activity, and in the middle of intense activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert. Read it twice, because it runs both ways. Silence with life inside it. Busyness with a desert inside it. Then he adds that this person has learned self-control and can't be shaken by what's happening around them. Now look back at the week and watch the pieces fit. It began in Chicago, with a young monk greeting a hall full of strangers as sisters and brothers, and reading an Upanishad line that called everyone children of immortal bliss. Then a frog in a well, and the reminder that every well is small. Then the books of work. The world as a moral gymnasium, where the giver says thank you. The fly in the honey, learning to drink without getting stuck. And yesterday, the parking lot, where character is built out of common actions. Every one of those is about the same skill: staying in the middle of the action without being swept off by it. That's what the desert inside the station is. Not escaping the noise. Being quiet enough within it to work well. And it raises an obvious question. How do you actually find that quiet? Karma Yoga mostly answers with work itself. But Vivekananda has another book that goes straight at the mind, and that's where we go next.
screen: `SILENCE WITH ACTIVITY INSIDE IT.` · `ACTIVITY WITH A DESERT INSIDE IT.` · `THE WEEK: CHICAGO, GYMNASIUM, HONEY, HABITS.` · `HOW DO YOU FIND THE QUIET?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. For the first part of the sit, let the world in: every sound, every itch, every thought about what's next. Don't push any of it away. Then, without changing anything outside, look for the still place underneath it, the part of you that is noticing all the noise and isn't noisy itself. Rest there for a few breaths while the sounds go on. If you pray, you can hold that stillness in a prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, whose ideal is a calm desert in the middle of the busiest street.
Your line: a desert in the busy street. Today, at the busiest moment of your day, find the desert for one breath, then go straight back to work. Day nine hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Hindus who follow Vivekananda's teaching on Karma Yoga describe aiming to stay inwardly calm while working fully, and his talks are read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

notes: Paraphrase of Vivekananda's English. Confirm the ideal-man passage ('in the midst of the greatest silence and solitude, finds the intensest activity, and in the midst of the intensest activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert'; 'he has learnt the secret of restraint') and its chapter (believed ch. 1, Karma-Yoga). Kept as paraphrase because the validator's quotation list does not include Vivekananda.
